Zone numbers on aircraft blueprints are used to locate parts, sections, and views when you have a large blueprint with numerous parts.
Wing Stations (W.S.) are measured left or right of the aircraft centerline or sometimes referenced to the root of the wing or horizontal stabilizer.
Water Lines (W.L.) are height measurements perpendicular from a horizontal plane located at a fixed location either at or below the fuselage.
Buttock or Butt Lines (B.L.) are width measurements left or right of the vertical centerline.
Fuselage Stations (F.S.) are numbered in inches from reference datum or some other point identified by the manufacturer to a point in or on the aircraft.
Aircraft measurements aft of Reference Datum are shown in terms of plus numbers; those forward of Reference Datum, in terms of negative numbers.
Reference Datum is the "Zero" measurement that serves as the basis for all aircraft longitudinal measurements. Reference Datum could be at, forward, or aft of the nose of the aircraft.
The first and most important reference line is called "Reference Datum".

The "Removed Sections" drawing is very similar to the revolved section drawing with the exception that there will be more than one cross-section involved. Usually the profile pictures will be displayed on one side of the main drawing instead of within the object.

A Revolved Section Drawing basically cuts an object in half and then displays what the cross-section looks like. The view helps the technician visualize the third dimension in a two-dimensional drawing..

The Exploded View drawing is used primarily in the illustrated parts breakdown/catalog manual and throughout most maintenance manuals. It helps the technician correlate how all of the parts are assembled and in what order...

In a Half Section Drawing, the slice extends only halfway across the object, leaving the other half of the object as an exterior view. Half section drawings are used especially with symmetrical (same shape on both sides) objects to show both the interior and exterior.xterior...

A Section or Sectional View is obtained by slicing away part of an object to show the shape and construction of the interior of the object at the slice. Sectional Views are used when the interior or hidden features of an object cannot be shown clearly by using only exterior views.

Detail View Drawings show only a part of the object but in greater detail and to a larger scale than the Principle View. These drawings are normally a part of another drawing and are identified by a heavy line encircling the object...

A complete view of an object is called the Principle View. Drawings usually do not show more than one Principle View on the same drawing. Instead the drawing will show one Principle View and one or more Detail or Sectional Views..

A Pictorial Drawing most resembles a photograph. It shows an object as it appears to the eye. Pictorial Drawings are excellent for use in maintenance, overhaul and part number publications, however, they do not show dimension or intricate shapes very well.
